is.t: Explain: the sizing planner in plain words
In plain words: what this workbook answers

Before a large deployment you need to know how much memory, disk and CPU one Drishti server needs, and which settings to give it. Type what you expect (positions, dates kept in memory, users, the Java version) into the yellow cells of Inputs; Results then gives, line by line, the heap each part takes, the -Xmx to set, the machine's RAM, the disk by folder, the cores, the exact configuration keys with their values, the JVM arguments ready to paste, and warnings in words when a choice is risky. Every figure is an Excel formula you can follow; every constant it uses is on Coefficients, with where it came from, so you can tune it when you measure your own server.
How to use it

1. Fill Inputs (yellow). 2. Read Results from the top: the heap terms, then the heap to set, page cache and RAM, disk, CPU, the settings and the JVM arguments; read every warning that is not OK. 3. Copy the settings into the server's configuration and the command line into its start script. 4. After the server runs with real data, compare Admin → Caches and Health with the lines here, and correct a coefficient (its status says how sure it is) when they differ. If your spreadsheet program does not recalculate on opening, press F9 (Excel) or Ctrl+Shift+F9 (LibreOffice).
Units
MB is 1,024 × 1,024 bytes and GB is 1,024 MB, as Java and Admin → Caches count them. Times are seconds.
Coefficients and their status

measured: read in a benchmark or a test (the source names the section). formula: a rule of the code or the guides (VAR_GUIDE.md, RESOURCES_AND_SCALE.md, CONFIGURATION.md). calibrated: set so that the defaults reproduce the 1,000,000-position re-benchmark (Java 21, 6 GB heap): BookHeapCalibration, FirstOpenOnceMB, BasePerPositionB, BaseTradeRows, HotSmallBytesPerTrade, LakeBytesPerValue, ResidentFirstIdle, ResidentNextIdle, ResidentShare, ExpHotBytesPerTrade, and ReqPerCoreVarAtRef from the users run. The users' figures are PerUserMB (working memory per concurrent user, measured) and ReqPerCoreTrades / ReqPerCoreVarAtRef (requests a second per core): change them in one place when you measure your own server. estimate: a reasoned guess to replace by a measurement.
Input: Positions a business date
How many positions one business date holds. Default: the production shape, OTC trades, one trade a position, so positions = trades. Default 300,000 (positions); named Positions.
Input: Trades a business date
How many trades those positions are made of. Default: production, about 300,000 trades. Default 300,000 (trades); named Trades.
Input: Trades per position, of positions that hold several
Only used when trades exceed positions: how many trades a shared (fungible) position holds on average. Default 2 (trades); named TradesPerFungible.
Input: Portfolios

Stored portfolios: baskets, rule portfolios, desk and book portfolios. Default: 300,000 ÷ 1,000,000 of the 1,000,000-position benchmark's 15,000 (desks and books grow with the positions: a desk holds 2,000 positions at both benchmark sizes, BENCHMARK.md 3). Default 4,500 (portfolios); named Portfolios.
Input: Basket members
Positions named by all the baskets together. Default: 300,000 ÷ 1,000,000 of the 1,000,000-position benchmark's 2,000,000. Default 600,000 (members); named BasketMembers.
Input: Hierarchy nodes

Nodes of every risk hierarchy (bank, legal entities, divisions, desks, limit letters...). Default: 300,000 ÷ 1,000,000 of the 1,000,000-position benchmark's 27,024. Default 8,107 (nodes); named Nodes.
Input: Books and cells
Trading books plus the cells of column hierarchies. Default: 300,000 ÷ 1,000,000 of the 1,000,000-position benchmark's 130,000. Default 39,000 (books + cells); named BooksCells.
Input: Scenarios
Scenario days in a P&L vector (509: two years of history plus the base). Default 509 (scenarios); named Scenarios.
Input: Trade currencies per node
On average, how many trade currencies a node's trades are in. Default 1 (currencies); named TradeCcysPerNode.
Input: Years of business dates kept in the lake
How much history the lake keeps (the bank's rule is often 7 years). Default 1 (years); named LakeYears.
Input: Dates in memory (hot-dates)
Business dates kept open at once; the least recently used one leaves first. Default 10 (dates); named HotDates.
Input: Pinned dates kept in memory
Dates that must always stay open (a month-end the desks compare with, an audit date). Default 0 (dates); named PinnedMem.
Input: Pinned dates kept on disk
Dates whose hot file is always kept on local disk, so they open in a second (month-ends, year-ends). Default 0 (dates); named PinnedDisk.
Input: Reporting currencies built ahead (besides USD)
Each one is a whole extra book a date (the shipped setting builds 4: EUR, CAD, JPY, GBP). Default 0 (currencies); named CcysAhead.
Input: Stress set on (1) or off (0)
1 when stressed VaR is used: the stress set is a book of its own a date. Default 0 (0 or 1); named StressOn.
Input: Intraday batches a day
Intraday batches applied to today's date. Default 10 (hourly over the trading day): assumed, confirm the batch count. Default 10 (batches); named IntradayBatches.
Input: Updates per intraday batch
Trades amended, added or cancelled in one batch. Default: 39% of the 300,000 trades a day (117,000) over the 10 batches. Default 11,700 (trades); named UpdatesPerBatch.
Input: Exposure on (1) or off (0)
1 when the counterparty exposure engine serves dates on this server. Default 0 (0 or 1); named ExposureOn.
Input: Netting sets
Netting sets a business date. Default 10,000 (sets); named NettingSets.
Input: Exposure trades
Trades with simulated paths a business date. Default 100,000 (trades); named ExpTrades.
Input: Paths
Monte Carlo paths a trade. Default 200 (paths); named Paths.
Input: Time steps
Grid dates of a path. Default 24 (grid dates); named TimeSteps.
Input: Exposure dates in memory
drishti.ccr.exposure.hot-dates: exposure dates kept open. Default 10 (dates); named ExpHotDates.
Input: Trade and BI rows a day
Trade rows loaded a business date, all trade systems together. Default: the same 300,000 production trades, served as trades too. Default 300,000 (rows); named TradeRowsPerDay.
Input: Days of trade rows kept
Business days of trades kept in the lake (252 is a year). Default 252 (days); named TradeDaysKept.
Input: Trade connectors
Trade systems read through their own connector (for example ENDUR, CALYPSO, MUREX). Default 3 (connectors); named TradeConnectors.
Input: Concurrent users
People (or programs) asking questions at the same moment at the busiest time. Default 50 (users); named Users.
Input: Peak requests a second wanted
Requests a second the server must answer at the peak. Default 100 (requests/s); named PeakRps.
Input: Share of VaR questions
Of those requests, the share that are VaR questions (the rest are trades, searches, pages). Default 0.5 (share); named VarShare.
Input: Java version (21 or 25)
The Java the server runs on; 25 adds compact object headers. Default 21 (21 or 25); named JavaVersion.
Input: Load threads (drishti.var.load-threads)
Dates that may load from the lake at the same time. Default 2 (threads); named LoadThreads.
Input: Garbage collector: auto, G1 or ZGC
auto follows the documented rule: generational ZGC from 16 GB of heap, G1 below. Default auto (text); named Collector.
Input: Data folder
Where Drishti keeps everything it writes (dumps, logs and temporary files go under it). Default /opt/drishti/data (path); named DataFolder.
Input: Server jar
The server's jar, as the command line starts it. Default drishti-server-{VERSION}-exec.jar (file); named ServerJar.
Heap: one VaR book

A business date's VaR data lives in three places: the lake (every date, on disk), a hot file (one per open date, on local disk, mapped into memory: the P&L rows) and the heap (the date's ids, columns, nodes and links). The heap of one book is VAR_GUIDE.md section 27.1's H_book, term by term: node members as runs (8·R), names and runs (~150 bytes a book, cell or node), the aggregates' index (64·A), the columns (108·T + 136·P), the ids (72·(2T + 3P), the largest part), the per-currency totals of every node (8·(S+1)·N·C) and the portfolios. The sum is scaled by BookHeapCalibration to what the server measured.
Heap: one date and the dates in memory

A date is its USD book plus one book per reporting currency built ahead and one for the stress set. The server keeps hot-dates dates open; the date just used, the newest date and the dates pinned in memory always stay, so if those alone are more than hot-dates, the planner counts them instead. While a new date opens, the date it pushes out stays open until the requests reading it finish, so the peak is one date more.
Heap: the server, caches and users

At start, before any date is open, the server already holds the lake's footers and an index of the P&L rows (HeapBase, measured). The first date opened warms caches once (HeapFirstOpen). Each cache is counted at its budget: the Parquet footer cache, the type-ahead index, BI's query and plan caches, the history answers and VaR's answers. Trade rows beyond those measured add the trade connectors' working set, and each concurrent user's request needs working memory (PerUserMB, measured: about 2.5 MB).
Heap: loads in progress

While a date loads, the build holds its aggregates and currency totals on the heap (1.6 GB at 1,000,000 positions, VarProperties) plus a read buffer; drishti.var.load-threads dates may load at once. An exposure load holds every netting set's value matrix in float64.
The heap to set (-Xmx)

The collector needs room: the heap after collection should be at most 61% of -Xmx (RESOURCES_AND_SCALE.md 9.5). So -Xmx = the steady heap ÷ 0.61 + the loads in progress, rounded up to a whole GB. Under 32 GB Java keeps 4-byte object references (compressed oops); at 32 GB and above they double in size unless -XX:ObjectAlignmentInBytes=16, which keeps them compressed up to 64 GB: so either stay at 31g or go well past 32.
Page cache and RAM

The hot files are read through the operating system's page cache, outside the heap: a question over the whole bank reads every row of a date. Recommended RAM keeps every open date's hot files resident, plus the heap (fully committed after a while), native memory (metaspace, direct buffers, threads, the allocator), the operating system and the console. The smallest workable RAM keeps only the date being read resident: it works, but a question on another date reads the disk first.
Disk, by folder

The lake keeps every date for the years you keep; var/hot keeps up to 60 hot files (disk-dates) plus the pinned dates on disk and currency books for the 5 newest dates; tmp/server needs three times the largest hot file for each load running (the disk guard checks this before a build); logs rotate; a heap dump is the heap's size; the trade connectors keep id maps, grouped pages, a document cache and the type-ahead index; BI keeps layers and runs. The recommendation leaves the free-space guard's margin: 10% of the disk and 20 GB free. When the lakes live on object storage, the local-disk line is the one to buy fast (NVMe).
CPU

Each core answers about 22.5 trade questions a second and, at 1,000,000 positions, about 11.6 VaR questions a second (measured on a machine of 12 cores and 24 hardware threads: 183 requests a second at 50 users, half of them VaR, none failed). A VaR question's cost grows with the positions (VarCostExponent). The mix is weighed by your share of VaR questions; the cores (physical cores, two hardware threads each) are planned 70% busy at the peak, plus 2 for loads, the collector and the operating system. More users than the cores can serve do not fail, they wait: the same machine answered 138 requests a second at 100 users and 124 at 200, with p95 about 2 and 5 s.
The settings

drishti.var.hot-dates: the dates in memory. drishti.var.open-heap-mb: the byte safety net over every open date's heap; when the dates open exceed it, the least recently used dates' currency books, then stress books, then whole dates close (never a protected one, never one read in the last 120 seconds). Its automatic value (0.4 × heap − 512 MB − load-threads × 1.6 GB) is often smaller than ten dates need, so the planner gives an explicit value. drishti.var.memory-budget-mb bounds the heap tier only and stays 0 on the mapped tier. -Ddrishti.parquet.footer-cache-mb is a JVM property. drishti.var.load-threads, drishti.var.tier.max-disk-gb, disk-dates, currencies, stress and the exposure dates follow. Each setting is given in its three forms with its exact key, as CONFIGURATION.md names it: YAML for ./application.local.yaml in the server's working directory (the recommended form), the environment variable (CONFIGURATION.md's name, or Spring's relaxed binding of the key when it names none: drop the dashes, dots to underscores, upper case) and the server argument (--key=value). The YAML block to paste merges them under one drishti: root. The JVM arguments (-X, -XX and the -D system properties the code reads) are command line only, not YAML; they may also go in JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS. MALLOC_ARENA_MAX is an environment variable of Linux.
JVM: -Xmx
The heap computed above. When: always. (documented: from the docs and launchers.)
JVM: -Xms
The whole heap reserved and committed from the start: no growth pauses, and RSS is known from day one. When: a server. (suggested: beyond the docs, a suggestion.)
JVM: Collector

ZGC pauses under a millisecond whatever the heap; G1 costs less on a small heap. Measured: ZGC doubled RSS at the same -Xmx and stalled allocations at 200,000 positions; choose G1 (Collector) when RAM is tight. When: heap ≥ 16 GB: ZGC; Java 21 needs -XX:+ZGenerational. (documented: from the docs and launchers.)
JVM: Collector tuning
ZGC collects early to stay under 80% of the heap (planned in the docs); G1's periodic collection returns unused memory. When: ZGC: 0.8 × heap; G1: always. (documented: from the docs and launchers.)
JVM: -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis
The docs give no pause goal; G1's default (200 ms) stays. When: not set. (documented: from the docs and launchers.)
JVM: -XX:ObjectAlignmentInBytes
Keeps 4-byte references above 32 GB, at the cost of padding objects to 16 bytes; or stay at 31g. When: heap over 31 GB, up to 64 GB. (suggested: beyond the docs, a suggestion.)
JVM: -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders
Smaller object headers, a little less heap. When: Java 25 only (21 refuses to start with it). (documented: from the docs and launchers.)
JVM: -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch
Not proposed by the docs: a slow start, and the whole heap committed at once. When: not set. (documented: from the docs and launchers.)
JVM: -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize
Caps direct buffers (the default cap is the heap's size). When: always. (documented: from the docs and launchers.)
JVM: -XX:TrimNativeHeapInterval
Returns freed native memory to the system every minute. When: Java 21.0.1 and later. (documented: from the docs and launchers.)
JVM: -Djdk.nio.maxCachedBufferSize
Stops each thread keeping a large temporary direct buffer after a read. When: always. (documented: from the docs and launchers.)
JVM: -XX:NativeMemoryTracking
Lets jcmd split native memory by category; a few per cent of overhead. When: always. (documented: from the docs and launchers.)
JVM: -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize
A ceiling well above the 131 MB measured, so a class leak fails loudly instead of growing; the code cache keeps its default. When: always. (suggested: beyond the docs, a suggestion.)
JVM: -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
A heap dump when the heap runs out, under the data folder; the disk lines keep room for it. When: always. (documented: from the docs and launchers.)
JVM: -Xlog:gc*
A rotated GC log (5 × 20 MB). When: always. (documented: from the docs and launchers.)
JVM: -Djava.io.tmpdir
Native libraries unpack and temporary files go under the data folder. When: always. (documented: from the docs and launchers.)
JVM: -Ddrishti.parquet.footer-cache-mb
The Parquet footer cache computed above. When: always. (documented: from the docs and launchers.)
JVM: -Ddrishti.open-dates.net-grace-seconds
The byte safety net never closes a date read in the last 120 s (closing it would reload it at once). When: always. (documented: from the docs and launchers.)
JVM: virtual-thread flags
-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full is a diagnostic only; the scheduler's parallelism keeps its default (the cores). When: not set. (documented: from the docs and launchers.)
JVM: --enable-native-access
The server jar's manifest already grants native access; no --add-opens is needed. When: not set with -jar. (documented: from the docs and launchers.)
JVM: MALLOC_ARENA_MAX (environment)
Two malloc arenas, not one per busy thread: about 500 MB less RSS measured. When: Linux (glibc) only. (documented: from the docs and launchers.)
The command line

Results assembles every argument into one line ready to paste: MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 java <arguments> -jar <the server jar>. On Windows leave out MALLOC_ARENA_MAX (a Linux setting) and use Windows paths for the data folder.
Examples: two shapes

The two examples below are the workbook's results for two sets of inputs: the defaults (the production shape) and the 1,000,000-position benchmark. Type either into Inputs to see every line; the Calibration check block always shows the benchmark against what it measured.
Example 1, production (the defaults): 300,000 trades, 39% updated intraday

300,000 OTC trades, one a position; portfolios, basket members, nodes, books and cells scaled from the benchmark by 0.3; 10 intraday batches of 11,700 updates (117,000 a day, 39% of the trades; the batch count assumed); 300,000 trade rows a day; 10 dates in memory; 50 users and 100 requests a second, half VaR; Java 21. One book is 217 MB of heap (223 by the formula, calibrated); the dates in memory and one opening take 2,383 MB; today's intraday layer 1,627 MB. The steady heap after GC is 5,305 MB and the loads in progress add 1,367 MB: -Xmx = 5,305 ÷ 0.61 + 1,367, rounded up: -Xmx10g, collector G1. drishti.var.open-heap-mb 4,032 (the automatic net would be 1,024 MB). A hot file is 898 MB a date; the open dates' page cache 6,699 MB. RAM 24 GB recommended (16 GB the smallest workable). Disk: the VaR lake for a year 106 GB, intraday batches in it 41.3 GB, hot files 52.6 GB, 375 GB in all: 450 GB recommended, 150 GB of local disk if the lakes live elsewhere. CPU: 8 cores. A date's first open about 5.5 s.
Example 2, the benchmark: 1,000,000 positions, no intraday

1,000,000 positions of one trade, 15,000 portfolios, 2,000,000 basket members, 27,024 nodes, 130,000 books and cells, no intraday batch, 20,000 trade rows a day; the rest as the defaults. One book is 722 MB of heap (744 by the formula, calibrated); the dates in memory and one opening take 7,942 MB; today's intraday layer 0 MB. The steady heap after GC is 9,240 MB and the loads in progress add 3,328 MB: -Xmx = 9,240 ÷ 0.61 + 3,328, rounded up: -Xmx19g, collector ZGC. drishti.var.open-heap-mb 8,000 (the automatic net would be 4,070 MB). A hot file is 2,994 MB a date; the open dates' page cache 22,331 MB. RAM 48 GB recommended (32 GB the smallest workable). Disk: the VaR lake for a year 353 GB, intraday batches in it 0 GB, hot files 175 GB, 604 GB in all: 700 GB recommended, 300 GB of local disk if the lakes live elsewhere. CPU: 12 cores. A date's first open about 18.5 s.
Against the measured

The Calibration check block computes the benchmark shape from the Bench coefficients against the final 1,000,000-position users run at 6 GB of heap (measured in brackets): heap after GC 769 MB at start (769), 1,491 MB with one date open (1,352: every date is counted at the 0.72 GB average, the safe side), 2,213 MB with two (2,213); RSS 2,875, 5,156 and 6,899 MB (2,875, 5,156, 6,899); 2.8 GB of lake for two dates (2.8); 2,336 MB warm at 50 users (2,336), RSS 11,681 MB at the end (11,160) and 183 requests a second on its 12 cores (183.3). A recommended -Xmx is larger than the 6 GB that held two dates because it adds ten dates, the loads running together, every cache at its budget, the users and the collector's headroom.
Limits

One server only: a sharded cluster divides the hot files, the page cache and the loads among its members but copies each date's skeleton to every member, which this sheet does not model; a cluster sheet comes later. The requests a second per core were measured on one workstation; a server's cores may differ. The hot files' page cache is advisory: the server works with less RAM, more slowly. The figures are for the mapped tier (the default); the heap tier keeps every vector on the heap (HeapTierBudgetMB a date).
